goals: Understand runoff generation mechanisms across Naches heterogeneity (elevation, soil)
Quantify partitioning between surface runoff and subsurface drainage
Identify dominant runoff pathways in different landscape positions

model_choice.rationale: Runoff generation is a spatially heterogeneous process driven by elevation (snow/precip) and soil (infiltration). A site-based stratified design isolates these controls across the Naches domain.

answerable: Column-scale surface runoff and subsurface drainage partitioning across soil types
Soil texture control on infiltration and runoff generation (holding forcing constant)
Temporal dynamics of runoff generation (seasonal, event-scale)

not_answerable.aspect: Elevation/climate control on runoff generation (snow vs rain dominance)
not_answerable.why: Uniform forcing across all columns—elevation does not modulate precipitation or temperature in the current stack
not_answerable.needs: Elevation-downscaled meteorological forcing (precip lapse rate, temperature lapse rate)

not_answerable.aspect: Watershed-scale runoff generation and validation against USGS stream gauges
not_answerable.why: ELM produces column-scale fluxes (surface runoff, QDRAI) but no lateral routing or aggregation to outlet
not_answerable.needs: Runoff routing and aggregation to HUC outlet for gauge comparison

not_answerable.aspect: Spatial patterns of runoff contribution (where in the watershed runoff is generated)
not_answerable.why: No mechanism to aggregate or map column fluxes to watershed-scale patterns
not_answerable.needs: Spatial aggregation and visualization of distributed column outputs

sampling_strategy.approach: stratified by elevation and soil, with concentration in runoff-generating zones
sampling_strategy.n_justification: 3 elevation bands × 2 soil classes × 3 replicates = 18 columns. Three replicates per stratum provide light spatial variability within each combination while keeping total N manageable. This resolves the soil-runoff mechanism (answerable) and sets up the elevation structure for future forcing downscaling (currently not answerable).
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Concentrate columns in mid-elevation rain-snow transition zone (900-1400 m) and valley bottoms/riparian corridors where saturation-excess runoff is most likely. Avoid ridge tops and steep slopes where ELM's 1-D assumption is weakest. Sample across aspect (N vs S facing) within elevation bands to capture solar radiation effects on snowmelt timing.
sampling_strategy.replication: 3 replicates per stratum to capture within-stratum spatial variability in soil properties and topographic position, supporting robust stratum-level statistics.

sampling_plan.reason: Rain-dominated zone with sandy soils—tests infiltration-excess runoff under high-intensity rain events
Rain-dominated zone with fine-textured soils—tests saturation-excess runoff and soil moisture persistence
Rain-snow transition with sandy soils—tests snowmelt infiltration and subsurface drainage dominance
Rain-snow transition with fine-textured soils—tests saturation-excess runoff from snowmelt on low-permeability substrate
Snow-dominated zone with sandy soils—tests delayed snowmelt infiltration and recharge timing
Snow-dominated zone with fine-textured soils—tests surface runoff from snowmelt on frozen or saturated ground

validation_design.observation_source: USGS stream gauges at HUC outlet
validation_design.comparison: aggregated—requires routing column fluxes to outlet, currently not possible
validation_design.metric: Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE), percent bias, flow duration curve comparison
validation_design.n_validation_points: 1 gauge at outlet (aggregated validation, not co-located)

validation_design.comparison: analog—compare ELM SWE dynamics to nearby SNOTEL time series for process validation of snow accumulation/melt timing
validation_design.metric: Peak SWE timing, melt rate, seasonal correlation
validation_design.n_validation_points: unknown—depends on SNOTEL station density near Naches

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: Baseline forcing (uniform across domain, 1980-2018 available), native soil properties from gridded soil dataset

assumptions: Uniform meteorological forcing across all columns (no elevation downscaling)—elevation stratification captures spatial structure but not climate gradient
Gridded soil dataset exists and provides texture/hydraulic properties at column resolution
DEM exists at sufficient resolution (~30-90 m) to extract elevation, slope, aspect for placement
USGS gauge at HUC outlet has continuous streamflow record during 1980-2018 forcing period
ELM's 1-D column assumption is acceptable for the sampled locations (avoid steep slopes, complex terrain)
Subsurface drainage (QDRAI) is a reasonable proxy for baseflow contribution to streamflow, though it exits the column bottom without lateral routing
